passage:
In their village near Sangli, Darshan had studied under the solar bulb until past midnight three nights running. On Thursday morning he shouted at his sister Vidya for moving his pen, then sat at breakfast unable to remember the formula he had learned the day before. His eyes filled. "I'm useless," he whispered. "I'm turning into a horrible person."
Amma put down the ladle and looked at his dark eyes. "You're tired, that's all," said Vidya, no longer angry.
"Tonight the light goes off at ten," said Amma. "The books will still be here. And if you still feel like this after proper sleep, we'll speak to your teacher together."
That night he slept, and on the bus next day the formula wandered back like a lost goat.

qa.q: Where did Darshan study at night?
qa.a: Under the solar bulb.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling at breakfast?
qa.a: Ashamed and overwhelmed. His eyes filled, and he whispered that he was useless and turning into a horrible person.

qa.q: What choice did Amma make that helped Darshan?
qa.a: Amma noticed his dark eyes and made the light go off at ten, saying the books would wait, and offered to talk to the teacher if the feeling stayed.

qa.q: How does Vidya see Darshan's shouting after breakfast?
qa.a: Vidya stops being angry and sees it as tiredness. She says, 'You're tired, that's all.'

grounding: A teenager short of sleep becomes irritable and foggy and thinks it is a personality flaw.

passage:
Nazia, come here. Your Nani Ishita has something to tell you before your board exams.
In my Class 12, my whole hostel room crammed all night. I kept three things: bed at a fixed hour, a walk to the mango tree after dinner, and a proper meal. My friends laughed at me, and I felt silly for a day, but I kept my three. On the morning of the physics paper, half of them stared at the questions with blank faces. I remembered the derivation as if it were written on the wall.
I am not saying study less. I am saying the hour you save by not sleeping is often the hour you lose in the exam hall. Take your walk, beta.

qa.q: What three things did Ishita keep during exam season?
qa.a: A fixed bedtime, a walk to the mango tree after dinner, and a proper meal.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel when friends laughed, and what did Ishita do?
qa.a: Ishita felt a little silly for a day but kept the three habits anyway.

qa.q: What choice did young Ishita make that paid off on the day of the physics paper?
qa.a: Ishita kept sleep, a walk and a meal on schedule while others crammed all night, and remembered the derivation clearly.

qa.q: How might Ishita's friends have felt on the morning of the physics paper?
qa.a: Probably anxious and foggy, since half of them stared at the questions with blank faces after cramming all night.

grounding: An elder recalls keeping sleep, a walk and a meal during exams and remembering better than friends who crammed.

The chemistry paper was at nine the next morning, the corridor throbbed with someone's speaker, and Jasleen was waving a highlighter. "Sleep is a luxury tonight," she said. "We study till dawn."
Indu closed her notes at half past nine. She had already eaten a proper dinner and walked once round the hostel garden, listening to frogs. "If I can't answer it now, two more hours won't fix it," she said, and set her alarm.
Jasleen scoffed, but by midnight she was rereading the same page. In the hall Indu's mind was clear; she recalled the reaction steps in order and even had time to check. Jasleen yawned through the last question.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel as midnight passes and she rereads the same page?
qa.a: Probably anxious and tired, since she is stuck on the same page and yawns through the last question.

grounding: A student in exam season keeps sleep, a walk and a meal on schedule despite noise and time pressure.

passage:
Every Sunday in the kasba, Urmila's phone lived in the kitchen drawer. She had learned the hard way, after a month of seven working days and a cry over a leaking tap, that rest isn't something you earn after collapsing. Now Sunday meant a late breakfast with her mother Charu, a slow walk to the river bridge, and a nap with no alarm.
That afternoon the drawer glowed with a message from her manager. Urmila glanced at it, wrote "Monday, 9 a.m." on a slip of paper, and went back to shelling peas.
"You're not answering?" asked Charu.
"Tomorrow," said Urmila. "That's what Sundays are for."

qa.q: Where did Urmila keep her phone on Sundays?
qa.a: In the kitchen drawer.

qa.q: What did Urmila feel about resting, and what showed it?
qa.a: She felt firm and unashamed about it. She learned the hard way that rest is not something to earn after collapsing, and she leaves her manager's message for Monday.

qa.q: What choice did Urmila make when the manager's message arrived?
qa.a: She noted 'Monday, 9 a.m.' on a slip of paper and went on shelling peas instead of answering.

qa.q: What might Charu think when Urmila does not answer the message?
qa.a: Charu seems surprised and curious, asking if Urmila is not answering, and may see that her daughter's Sundays are deliberately protected.

grounding: A young worker builds a real weekly day off and treats rest as prevention, not a reward.

Jana put three things in her calendar in ink every week, like meetings she could not move: an early finish on Wednesday, an unhurried lunch on Saturday with no screens, and one full day off when the work phone stayed in a drawer.
Her flatmate Ines teased her at first. "You're not even tired," she said.
"That's the point," said Jana, slicing bread. "I do it while I'm fine, so I don't have to crash and call it a holiday."
When her manager in Lisbon asked for a weekend favour, Jana said, "I can do it Monday morning." The world did not end. On Sunday evening she felt ready, not relieved.

qa.q: What three things did Jana put in her calendar?
qa.a: An early finish on Wednesday, an unhurried lunch on Saturday with no screens, and one full day off.

qa.q: How does Jana feel about protecting her rest?
qa.a: Steady and unapologetic. She rests while she is fine, so she will not have to collapse first.

qa.q: What did Jana say to her manager, and what happened?
qa.a: She offered Monday morning instead of the weekend, and nothing bad happened; she felt ready, not relieved, on Sunday evening.

qa.q: How might Ines see Jana's calendar at first?
qa.a: As odd, because Jana is not even tired. Ines teases her, though Jana's answer suggests it is prevention.

grounding: A young worker builds weekly rest into her calendar as an ongoing practice rather than a reward after collapse.

At the birthday party in the society hall, Yamini slipped out with her book and settled into the quiet corner behind the sofa. Music thumped, balloons burst. She turned a page, feet tucked up, smiling at nothing.
Her mother Vidya found her and crouched. "Everyone's playing musical chairs, beta. Don't you want to?"
"Not now," said Yamini. "I'm at the best part."
Vidya looked at her calm face, then at the noisy room. "Shall I bring you a plate?"
"Yes, please."
When the game ended, Yamini strolled over on her own, cheeks pink, and asked what the next round was.

qa.q: Where did Yamini settle with her book?

qa.a: She feels content. She smiles at nothing, tucks her feet up and says she is at the best part.

qa.q: What choice by Vidya helped Yamini's afternoon?
qa.a: Vidya looked at Yamini's calm face, did not force her to join and offered to bring a plate instead.

qa.q: What might Vidya have been thinking as she looked at the noisy room?

Usha Madam had taught at the village school for years, and every recess she saw Elizabeth on the same stone bench under the tamarind tree, reading. The other teachers whispered, "She's too quiet. Someone should push her to play."
Usha wasn't sure. One day she sat down and asked gently, "Are you all right? Would you like to join the skipping?"
Elizabeth looked up, surprised. "I'm fine, Madam. I like this part of the book. I play with Malar on Fridays."
Her eyes were bright, not wary. On Friday Usha watched Malar arrive and Elizabeth put the book down, laughing. She told the others, "Let's keep watching, but let her be. If she stops eating or stops smiling, we speak to her family."

qa.q: Where did Elizabeth sit during recess?
qa.a: On a stone bench under the tamarind tree.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling as the other teachers whispered about Elizabeth?
qa.a: Usha felt unsure and a little concerned. She did not want to push, but wanted to check that all was well.

qa.q: What choice did Usha make instead of pushing Elizabeth into games?
qa.a: Usha sat down, asked gently if Elizabeth was all right and watched on Friday, keeping a plan to speak to the family if signs of trouble appeared.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth see her recess reading?
qa.a: She sees it as something she enjoys and is fine with, and says she plays with Malar on Fridays.

grounding: Adults worry when a quiet child prefers being alone, and a teacher checks gently before deciding it is temperament.

Bilal watched his daughter Xin sit alone on the apartment steps in Toronto with her bird book while the other children kicked a ball. He felt a small knot in his chest. On Saturday he signed her up for the football club. "You'll make friends!" he said.
Xin shrugged. On the way home he asked, "Do you have someone to talk to at school?"
"Yes," she said. "Mei and Oscar. But I like Saturdays with my birds."
He noticed she was chatting, not dodging. "Are you happy?"
"Yes, Baba. Can I go to the club only on some days?"
He took a breath. "Some days," he said, and carried her bird book for her.

qa.q: Where did Xin sit while the other children kicked a ball?
qa.a: On the apartment steps, with her bird book.

qa.q: What was Bilal feeling as he watched Xin sit alone?
qa.a: Bilal felt worried, a small knot in his chest, and wanted her to have friends.

qa.q: What turning point changed Bilal's plan for Xin?
qa.a: He asked whether she had someone to talk to and whether she was happy, listened to her answers and agreed to football only on some days.

qa.q: How does Xin seem to feel about her Saturdays alone with her birds?
qa.a: She seems content. She names two school friends and says she likes Saturdays with her birds.

grounding: Adults worry when a quiet child prefers being alone, and a father checks for real distress and finds temperament.

Pooja had shut her bedroom door at four, and by seven she still couldn't tell why. Some evenings the quiet felt like a warm bath: music low, sketchbook open, everyone's noise far away. Tonight the same quiet felt like a closed window. She heard laughter from the living room, and her chest pulled toward it and away at once.
A knock. Her brother Vikas said through the door, "Tea?"
She almost said no. Instead she opened the door a crack, took the cup and said, "I think I'm a bit lonely. Or maybe I just need to be by myself. I can't tell."
"Company or quiet?"
"Can you sit in the doorway?"
He sat on the floor, back against the frame, and said nothing until she did.

qa.q: What time had Pooja shut her bedroom door?
qa.a: At four.

qa.q: What is Pooja feeling that she cannot name?
qa.a: She is torn between wanting quiet and aching for company. Her chest pulls toward the laughter and away from it at once, and she says she cannot tell which it is.

qa.q: What small step did Pooja take that helped?
qa.a: She opened the door a crack, took the tea and told Vikas she might be lonely, then asked him to sit in the doorway.

qa.q: How does Vikas seem to read the closed door?
qa.a: He does not assume. He knocks with tea, asks whether she wants company or quiet, and sits silently until she is ready to talk.

grounding: A teenager alone in her room is unsure whether she is recharging or aching for connection.

Counsellor's note, Tanvir. Zainab, fifteen, came in after her mother phoned the school about her "shutting herself in." Zainab said she keeps her door closed to write and think, and that last week she found her mother reading her diary and checking her phone. She feels "watched, like a suspect," and now answers in single words at home.
Nothing she described points to danger; she talks about friends and her writing. I will meet her mother tomorrow, share only what Zainab agrees to, and suggest a knock, a cup of tea and being around instead of questions. If Zainab's mood or routine changes, I will follow up at once.

Tuesday night. Something good happened today. When I came home I went straight to my room and shut the door. A month ago Amma would have knocked five times and asked, "What happened? Tell me!" Today she knocked once and said, "Tea's on the table when you want it. I'm in the kitchen." Then nothing.
My little brother Yash tried to peek through the keyhole, and Amma called him away: "Let her be."
I sat on my bed and wrote a poem nobody will read. By seven I was hungry and chatty, so I came out on my own and told Amma about the maths test before she asked. Maybe privacy isn't the opposite of closeness.
Sudha

grounding: A teenager wants a closed door and no questions, and is respected while a parent stays quietly available.

People ask me, "Gargi, how did you know?" I didn't know. I noticed. Farida used to be first to reply in our group chat, and then she stopped. Three Friday dinners in a row her seat stayed empty and I got "busy, next time."
At first I sent long worried messages and got nothing back. So I changed. I sent a photo of the dosa place she likes with "No need to reply, thinking of you." Then a voice note about my own terrible week.
A fortnight later: "Sorry I went quiet. Coffee?" Sitting there, she said things had felt heavy for a while. I said that if it stays heavy, someone trained to help could be worth trying, and I'd come along to the first visit if she wanted. I didn't push. I just kept leaving the door ajar.

qa.a: Three Friday dinners in a row.

qa.a: Gargi noticed and worried, but was not sure why. At first Gargi pushed with long messages, then softened when nothing came back.

qa.a: Gargi sent a photo of the dosa place with a note saying no need to reply, and then a voice note about Gargi's own week.

qa.a: She may have felt remembered without being pressured, which could be why she replied later and said things had felt heavy.

I'm Aadhya, and I share the pantry table with Joseph. He used to eat lunch with us, then started saying "I'll skip today," then stopped coming to the Friday quiz, and lately his replies on our team chat arrive a day late and one line long. I can't tell why, and it might just be a busy stretch. But nobody had checked in, so I left a mug of tea at his desk with a note: "No need to talk. The pantry table's yours whenever."
